title: 2 Chronicles 28:16–27
context: Under pressure from Edom and the Philistines, Ahaz appeals to the kings of Assyria. Tilgath-pilneser comes but gives him trouble and does not help, despite the tribute Ahaz pays. Ahaz then sacrifices to the gods of Damascus, cuts up the vessels of God’s house, shuts its doors, and builds altars throughout Jerusalem and high places in every city. In 2 Kings 16:7-9 the Assyrian king listens, takes Damascus, and kills Rezin, and 2 Kings 16:10-18 describes the Damascus-style altar built by Urijah, which Chronicles does not mention. Chronicles also says Ahaz was not buried in the tombs of the kings, while 2 Kings 16:20 says he was buried with his fathers in David’s city. These differences are named, not resolved.

verses.text: At that time King Ahaz sent to the kings of Assyria to help him.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahaz sends to the kings of Assyria for help. Arminian readers see a king who, having refused to trust the LORD, turns to a foreign power; the Isaiah 7:9 box discusses the call to believe in this same crisis.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 2 Kings 16:7 names Tiglath Pileser and gives Ahaz’s words, I am your servant and your son. Chronicles summarizes the appeal briefly and focuses on its failure.

verses.text: For again the Edomites had come and struck Judah, and carried away captives.
verses.arminianNotes: The Edomites again strike Judah and carry away captives. Arminian readers see trouble multiplying for a king who had turned from God, as each new enemy exposes Judah’s weakness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Edomite attack is reported only in Chronicles. The Chronicler presents it as part of the pressure that drove Ahaz to Assyria and as further judgment.

verses.text: The Philistines also had invaded the cities of the lowland and of the South of Judah, and had taken Beth Shemesh, Aijalon, Gederoth, Soco with its villages, Timnah with its villages, and also Gimzo and its villages; and they lived there.
verses.arminianNotes: The Philistines invade the lowland and the South, taking towns and their villages. Arminian readers note that territory won under faithful kings is lost under an unfaithful one.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that this list of lost towns appears only in Chronicles. The losses reverse earlier gains against the Philistines and show the shrinking of Judah’s strength.

verses.text: For the LORD brought Judah low because of Ahaz king of Israel, because he acted without restraint in Judah and trespassed severely against the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD brought Judah low because Ahaz acted without restraint and trespassed severely. Arminian readers see a king’s choices bringing consequences on the whole nation he led.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Chronicles here calls Ahaz king of Israel, a usage the book sometimes applies to Judah’s kings. The verse gives the theological reason behind the military losses.

verses.text: Tilgath-pilneser king of Assyria came to him and gave him trouble, but didn’t strengthen him.
verses.arminianNotes: Tilgath-pilneser came to Ahaz and gave him trouble but did not strengthen him. Arminian readers see the bitter result of trusting a human power instead of God: the ally becomes another burden.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers name the difference from 2 Kings 16:9, where the Assyrian king listens, takes Damascus, and kills Rezin. Chronicles stresses that the alliance did not truly help Judah; the two accounts are left side by side.

verses.text: For Ahaz took away a portion out of the LORD’s house, and out of the house of the king and of the princes, and gave it to the king of Assyria; but it didn’t help him.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahaz takes treasure from the LORD’s house, the palace, and the princes for the king of Assyria, but it does not help. Arminian readers see sacred things spent on a strategy that failed.
verses.reformedNotes: The parallel at 2 Kings 16:8 also records the payment from the temple and palace. Chronicles adds the princes and the blunt verdict, it didn’t help him.

verses.text: In the time of his distress, he trespassed yet more against the LORD, this same King Ahaz.
verses.arminianNotes: In his distress Ahaz trespassed yet more against the LORD. Arminian readers see how affliction can harden rather than soften when a person refuses to turn, a choice that deepens ruin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the emphatic phrase, this same King Ahaz, marking him out. Hardship that should have led to repentance instead drove him further from God, a sober warning cited in the 2 Kings 16:19 notes.

verses.text: For he sacrificed to the gods of Damascus which had defeated him. He said, “Because the gods of the kings of Syria helped them, I will sacrifice to them, that they may help me.” But they were the ruin of him and of all Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahaz sacrificed to the gods of Damascus, reasoning that they had helped Syria’s kings. Arminian readers see a man choosing gods by apparent results, a calculation that proved fatal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Chronicles records this sacrifice, while 2 Kings 16:10-16 describes the altar copied from Damascus; Chronicles does not mention that altar. The gods were the ruin of him and of all Israel.

verses.text: Ahaz gathered together the vessels of God’s house, cut the vessels of God’s house in pieces, and shut up the doors of the LORD’s house; and he made himself altars in every corner of Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahaz cut the vessels of God’s house in pieces, shut its doors, and built altars in every corner of Jerusalem. Arminian readers see the deliberate closing of the place where Judah met with God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the shutting of the temple doors appears only in Chronicles, while 2 Kings 16:17-18 describes the removal of the bases, the sea, and the covered way. Hezekiah’s first act will be to reopen these doors (29:3).

verses.text: In every city of Judah he made high places to burn incense to other gods, and provoked the LORD, the God of his fathers, to anger.
verses.arminianNotes: In every city of Judah he made high places for other gods and provoked the LORD to anger. Arminian readers see a king using his power to spread idolatry throughout the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the Chronicler’s summary is sweeping. The worship of other gods is no longer confined to Jerusalem but fills the cities of Judah.

verses.text: Now the rest of his acts, and all his ways, first and last, behold, they are written in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: The rest of his acts and ways are written in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel. Arminian readers note that his ways, his moral direction, are the focus of the record.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the Chronicler’s reference to a fuller record, which differs in title from the source cited in 2 Kings 16:19. The verdict on Ahaz has already been given.

verses.text: Ahaz slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city, even in Jerusalem, because they didn’t bring him into the tombs of the kings of Israel; and Hezekiah his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahaz was buried in Jerusalem but not in the tombs of the kings. Arminian readers see a final mark of the nation’s judgment on a king who led them away from God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers set this beside 2 Kings 16:20, which says he was buried with his fathers in David’s city. Interpreters discuss the relation between the two notices; here they are named without resolution.
